--- title: "Random forests and boosting" description: "Two ways to combine many decision trees: a random forest averages trees grown on resampled data, and boosting adds small trees one after another, each fixing the errors of those before it." order: 6 categories: [supervised, trees-ensembles] --- ## Many trees instead of one A single [decision tree](decision-trees.qmd) is easy to read but unstable: a few different training examples can change its first question, and every question below it changes too. Combining many trees steadies the prediction, and there are two common ways to do it. A **random forest** grows many trees side by side and averages them. **Boosting** grows small trees one after another, each correcting the ones before it. This page shows both on the survey and compares them with a single tree and with Poisson regression from [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd). ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A random forest averages many trees Each tree in a forest is grown on a **bootstrap sample** of the training data: a sample of the same size drawn with replacement, so some examples appear twice or more and others not at all. Every tree therefore sees a slightly different dataset and asks slightly different questions. The forest's prediction is the average of all the trees' predictions. Where one tree guesses too high and another too low, the errors partly cancel. A forest adds one more source of variety. At each question, a tree may choose only among a few inputs picked at random, not among all of them. Without that rule, one strong input would open almost every tree, the trees would be too alike, and averaging them would gain little. The number of inputs to choose from is a setting called `mtry`; the usual default for a quantity is a third of the inputs. Adding trees to a forest makes its average steadier, up to a point where more trees change nothing. Too many trees cost computing time but do no harm. ## Boosting adds small trees in sequence Boosting starts from a simple prediction, such as the average outcome, and adds trees one at a time. Each new tree is fitted to the errors that remain: the gaps between the outcome and the current prediction. Its predictions are scaled down by a **learning rate**, such as 0.05, and added to the running total, so each tree corrects only a small part of what is still wrong. The trees are small, often only two or three questions deep, and the model's prediction is the sum of all of them. Every tree fits some of what the earlier trees missed, so the training error keeps falling as trees are added. Eventually the trees are fitting the noise, and the error on new data rises again. Unlike a forest, then, boosting has a number of trees that is too many, and it has to be chosen on validation data, as the depth of a single tree was. ::: {.diagram} ![One tree changes with its sample. A random forest averages many trees grown on resampled data; boosting adds small trees in sequence, each fitted to the errors left by those before it.](img/forest-and-boosting.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. One tree changes with its sample: three staircase predictions from trees fitted to slightly different samples of the same data step up at different places. A few different examples can change the first question and everything below it. Forest, average many trees: many faint staircases and their average, a thick line that rises more gradually. Each tree sees a resample of the examples and a few random inputs at each question. Boosting, small trees in sequence: three small trees in a row, each arrow labelled errors, and the prediction is the sum of all the trees, each scaled down. Each small tree fits what the trees before it got wrong. A note says adding trees to a forest stops helping but does no harm; boosting starts to overfit, so its number of trees is chosen on held-back data."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the fitting and validation sites are those of [Decision trees](decision-trees.qmd). The forest uses the same recipe as the single tree. xgboost, the package tidymodels uses for boosting, needs numbers only, so its recipe also turns each category into 0/1 columns. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) fit_split <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) fitting <- training(fit_split) validation <- testing(fit_split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) boost_recipe <- tree_recipe |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] inner = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) fit_rows, val_rows = next(inner.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) fitting, validation = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[val_rows] # scikit-learn's trees need numbers, so one recipe serves all three models. tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ], verbose_feature_names_out=False) def fit(model, data): return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]).fit( data[predictors], data["abundance"]) def rmse(fitted, data): return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], fitted.predict(data[predictors])) ``` ::: ::: ### One tree changes with its sample Six bootstrap samples of the training stations each grow a depth-3 tree, and the first question of each is printed. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree_model <- function(depth) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = depth, min_n = 2, cost_complexity = 0) } first_question <- function(data) { fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(3)) |> fit(data) labels(extract_fit_engine(fitted), digits = 3)[2] } samples <- bootstraps(train, times = 6) first_questions <- map_chr(samples$splits, \(s) first_question(analysis(s))) first_questions ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 5.7" "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 12.6" #> [3] "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 5.66" "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 2.57" #> [5] "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 5.71" "chlorophyll_mg_m3< 9.45" ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} names = tree_recipe.fit(train[predictors]).get_feature_names_out() rng = np.random.default_rng(123) for _ in range(6): sample = train.iloc[rng.integers(0, len(train), len(train))] tree = fit(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=123), sample) first = tree["model"].tree_ print(f"{names[first.feature[0]]} < {first.threshold[0]:.3g}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 < 1.74 #> temperature_c < 6.36 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 < 4.78 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 < 5.67 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 < 9.45 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 < 1.75 ``` ::: ::: ::: Every sample opens with a question about chlorophyll, but the threshold moves from 2.57 to 12.6 mg m⁻³. Each threshold sends different stations down each branch, so the questions below it differ too. The data barely changed; the tree changed a lot. ### Choosing the number of trees Forests and boosted models of 1 to 1600 trees are fitted on the fitting sites and scored on the validation sites. The forest keeps the defaults: a third of the inputs to choose from at each question, and leaves of at least five stations. The boosted trees are three questions deep with a learning rate of 0.05. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest_model <- function(trees) { rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = trees) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) } boost_model <- function(trees) { boost_tree(mode = "regression", trees = trees, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) } score <- function(recipe, model, trees) { fitted <- workflow(recipe, model) |> fit(fitting) error <- function(data) { rmse_vec(data$abundance, predict(fitted, data)$.pred) } tibble(trees = trees, training = error(fitting), validation = error(validation)) } sizes <- c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600) forest_scores <- map(sizes, \(n) score(tree_recipe, forest_model(n), n)) |> list_rbind() boost_scores <- map(sizes, \(n) score(boost_recipe, boost_model(n), n)) |> list_rbind() bind_rows(forest = slice_min(forest_scores, validation), boosting = slice_min(boost_scores, validation), .id = "model") |> mutate(across(c(training, validation), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | trees| training| validation| |:--------|-----:|--------:|----------:| |forest | 1600| 2.40| 3.77| |boosting | 200| 2.93| 3.79|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def forest_model(trees): # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=trees, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) def boost_model(trees): return GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=trees, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=123) def score(model, trees): fitted = fit(model, fitting) return {"trees": trees, "training": rmse(fitted, fitting), "validation": rmse(fitted, validation)} sizes = [1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600] forest_scores = pd.DataFrame([score(forest_model(n), n) for n in sizes]) boost_scores = pd.DataFrame([score(boost_model(n), n) for n in sizes]) pd.concat({ "forest": forest_scores.loc[[forest_scores["validation"].idxmin()]], "boosting": boost_scores.loc[[boost_scores["validation"].idxmin()]], }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> trees training validation #> forest 8 800 3.14 4.58 #> boosting 3 25 3.40 4.60 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_scores <- function(scores, title) { scores |> pivot_longer(c(training, validation), names_to = "data", values_to = "rmse") |> ggplot(aes(trees, rmse, colour = data)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_x_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = c(training = ml_palette[["blue"]], validation = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = "Number of trees (log scale)", y = "RMSE", colour = NULL, title = title) } plot_scores(forest_scores, "Forest: more trees stop helping") + plot_scores(boost_scores, "Boosting: too many trees fit the noise") + plot_layout(guides = "collect", axes = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The RMSE of forests and boosted models of each size on the stations they were fitted to and on the validation sites. The number of trees is on a log scale.](forests-and-boosting_files/figure-html/fig-trees-1.png){#fig-trees fig-alt='Two panels of RMSE against the number of trees, from 1 to 1600 on a log scale. In the forest panel both lines fall over the first few trees and then stay flat, the training line well below the validation line. In the boosting panel the training line falls steadily towards zero, while the validation line falls to a low point at a middle number of trees and then rises slowly.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: The forest's validation error falls from 4.59 with one tree to 3.8 with 100, and then barely moves: 3.77 with 1600. Its training error settles well below that, because every tree has seen most of the fitting stations. The page uses 400 trees from here on. Boosting behaves differently. Its training error falls with every tree added, to 0.61 at 1600 trees. Its validation error is lowest, 3.79, at 200 trees and rises after that, to 3.97 at 1600. The later trees are fitting chance patterns in the fitting sites, the overfitting a deep single tree showed. ### Averaging smooths the steps @fig-average draws 30 of the forest's 400 trees across temperature, with the other inputs held at typical values, and the forest's prediction, their average. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(0, 20, length.out = 400), depth_m = median(train$depth_m, na.rm = TRUE), chlorophyll_mg_m3 = median(train$chlorophyll_mg_m3, na.rm = TRUE), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu, na.rm = TRUE), substrate = factor("sand", levels = levels(train$substrate)), season = factor("summer", levels = levels(train$season)) ) each_tree <- predict(extract_fit_engine(forest_fit), grid, predict.all = TRUE)$predictions trees_long <- as_tibble(each_tree[, 1:30], .name_repair = \(x) paste0("tree", 1:30)) |> mutate(temperature_c = grid$temperature_c) |> pivot_longer(-temperature_c, names_to = "tree", values_to = ".pred") ggplot(trees_long, aes(temperature_c, .pred)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = temp_range[1], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + annotate("rect", xmin = temp_range[2], xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.12) + geom_line(aes(group = tree), colour = ml_palette[["orange"]], alpha = 0.35) + geom_line(data = augment(forest_fit, grid), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1.4) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count", title = "Each tree jumps; their average moves in small steps") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Predicted count across temperature from 30 of the forest's trees (thin lines) and from the whole forest (thick line), with the other inputs held at typical values (sand, summer, median depth, chlorophyll and salinity). The shaded ends lie beyond the temperatures of the training stations.](forests-and-boosting_files/figure-html/fig-average-1.png){#fig-average fig-alt='Thin orange staircases of predicted count against temperature from 0 to 20 degrees, each stepping up and down at different temperatures and some reaching far higher than others. A thick line through them, the forest\'s average, rises and falls in many small steps, with its highest values in the middle of the range. In the shaded regions beyond the training temperatures every line, including the average, stays level.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: A forest's trees are grown deep, so each is a jagged staircase with its own thresholds, and some reach far higher than the rest. Averaged, the large jumps shrink into many small steps. The average is still made of trees, though: beyond the warmest training station, at 16 °C, every tree stays level, and so does the forest. ### The ensembles on new sites The forest of 400 trees and the boosted model of 200 trees are refitted on all the training stations and scored once on the test sites. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} boost_fit <- workflow(boost_recipe, boost_model(best_boost)) |> fit(train) test_score <- function(fitted, model) { predicted <- predict(fitted, test)$.pred tibble(model = model, rmse = round(rmse_vec(test$abundance, predicted), 2), rsq = round(rsq_vec(test$abundance, predicted), 2)) } bind_rows(test_score(forest_fit, "forest"), test_score(boost_fit, "boosting")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| rsq| |:--------|----:|----:| |forest | 3.96| 0.11| |boosting | 4.35| 0.08|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} best_boost = int(boost_scores.loc[boost_scores["validation"].idxmin(), "trees"]) def test_score(fitted, model): predicted = fitted.predict(test[predictors]) return {"model": model, "rmse": root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], predicted), "rsq": np.corrcoef(predicted, test["abundance"])[0, 1] ** 2} pd.DataFrame([ test_score(fit(forest_model(400), train), "forest"), test_score(fit(boost_model(best_boost), train), "boosting"), ]).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> model rmse rsq #> 0 forest 4.77 0.32 #> 1 boosting 4.99 0.19 ``` ::: ::: ::: | Model | Test RMSE | Test $R^2$ | | --- | --- | --- | | Single tree, depth 5 | 4.48 | 0.04 | | Boosting, 200 trees | 4.35 | 0.08 | | Random forest, 400 trees | 3.96 | 0.11 | | Poisson regression | 3.55 | 0.24 | : The four models on the test sites. The single tree and Poisson regression are those of the two earlier pages. {#tbl-test} Both ensembles predict the test sites better than the single tree did, and the forest does best of the three, with an RMSE of 3.96 against the tree's 4.48. On the validation sites the order was the other way round: the tree scored 3.63 and the forest 3.77. A single tree fitted to one set of sites can happen to suit another small set, and the next set of sites shows how fragile that was. This is one more reason to judge models on several splits, as [Section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) does. Neither ensemble matches Poisson regression on this survey. About 600 noisy stations do not hold enough information for many trees to learn a shape that a smooth curve with a few terms describes as well. With far more stations, the balance can shift towards the ensembles. [Choosing a method](choosing-a-method.qmd) compares the section's models together. A forest or a boosted model cannot be printed and read like a single tree: its answer is the sum of hundreds of trees. [Section 10](../10-interpretation/index.qmd) covers ways to see which inputs such a model relies on and how its predictions change with each. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A single tree is unstable: resampling the survey kept the first input but moved its threshold from 2.57 to 12.6 mg m⁻³. - A random forest averages many trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample and choosing among a few random inputs at each question. Adding trees steadies it and never makes it worse. - Boosting adds small trees in sequence, each fitted to the remaining errors and scaled down by a learning rate. Too many trees fit the noise, so the number is chosen on validation data. - Averaging smooths a tree's steps, but a forest still stays level beyond the data. - On the test sites both ensembles beat the single tree, and neither beat Poisson regression. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Refit the boosted model with `learn_rate = 0.3`. How many trees give the lowest validation error now, and is that error lower or higher than with 0.05? 2. Set `mtry = 6` in `rand_forest()`, so every question may use any input, and score the forest of 400 trees on the validation sites. How much does the random choice of inputs matter here?
